headline: A really good business can produce disappointing returns if priced for perfection; a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if expectations were excessively pessimistic
reasoning: Investing is not a simple mathematical formula where good fundamentals mechanically produce good returns. What matters is how a company's earnings and fundamentals compare to the collective expectations already embedded in the share price. A high-quality company whose strong performance is already anticipated will see a stagnant or disappointing share price — as illustrated by employees who receive company shares and cannot understand why strong earnings produce no price gain. Conversely, a mediocre business can outperform if market expectations were excessively negative. This is the game-theory dimension of investing: outcomes depend not just on fundamentals but on the decisions and perceptions of all other market participants.
quote: And we're not saying that company earnings and other fundamentals don't matter. They of course do. But, it also matters how they compare to everyone else's expectations. And that really matters in terms of the outcome that you will achieve. So, really good business can produce disappointing investment returns if it's priced for perfection. On the other hand, a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if those expectations were excessively pessimistic.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

headline: Extreme pessimism in April 2025 tariff turmoil drove herd selling via loss aversion, while extreme optimism fuels bubble-buying — both are prisoner's-dilemma dynamics that destroy investor returns
reasoning: During the April 2025 tariff turmoil, investor sentiment surveys and the put/call ratio showed extreme pessimism, leading investors to sell en masse to avoid being 'left holding the bag.' This is driven by loss aversion — losses feel twice as painful as equivalent gains — causing selling that begets more selling. The mirror dynamic occurs in bubbles, where investors buy not because prices are justified but because they expect someone else to pay even more tomorrow. The key insight is that this behaviour doesn't require irrationality; it simply requires investors responding to their perception of the incentives they face. The optimal path — analogous to both prisoners staying silent — is for investors to remain patient during corrections, focus on fundamentals, and avoid portfolio decisions based on anticipating what everyone else will do.
quote: And what we see in the graph is extreme pessimism that often leads to large dips in the index where investors clamor to remove themselves before others do. They don't want to be the ones that are left holding the bag. And this is an example of the concept of loss aversion where a loss feels twice as painful as an equivalent gain. And then on the other side of that, of course, is when there's extreme optimism and that is when investors are trying to get into the market to capitalize on gains that they foresee before others do that. Now, imagine a world where more investors remain patient during a market correction. Share prices would likely recover much quicker and everyone would benefit. But instead, what we actually see in real life is that many investors sell because they fear others are going to sell and they're trying to get out of the market first.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

headline: Placed in the sin bin after three consecutive disappointments; retaining holding but unwilling to pay for earnings that have yet to arrive; material upside if Middle East conflicts resolve
reasoning: Worley has disappointed investors three times in quick succession — restructuring charges at the February result, a larger-than-expected Middle East and currency impact, and a weaker-than-anticipated FY27 outlook. Earnings quality is increasingly difficult to assess because underlying EBITA excludes approximately $120m of recurring restructuring costs, and procurement revenue (which grew ~35% at the first half) inflates reported turnover while contributing little incremental margin. Sustainability-related revenue has risen from one-third to nearly 70% of group revenue, yet FY26 group revenue was flat and underlying EBITA declined, breaking the expected nexus between sustainability exposure and shareholder value. The move into Full Project Delivery (EPC/EPCM) expands addressable spend but changes the risk profile by introducing execution complexity, lower margins and potential customer concentration. The firm will hold but is unwilling to capitalise earnings guided to arrive in six to twelve months; prices above approximately $13 are flagged as a likely reduction point. A resolution of Middle East conflicts is identified as the most material near-term upside catalyst.
quote: Worley is now in the sin bin. The FY27 outlook compounds our caution. Management expects growth, but earnings are again expected to be weighted towards the second half. After three disappointments in relatively quick succession, we are no longer prepared to capitalise earnings that management says will arrive in six or twelve months. For the next twelve months, Worley is effectively in our and the market's sin bin. This is not because we no longer believe in the underlying franchise. Rather, we have become tired of an attractive strategic story repeatedly being accompanied by earnings that arrive later, are lower than initially expected, or require another explanation. headline: SMSF succession planning is critical: cognitive decline, death and incapacity create structural and legal risks trustees must prepare for while still capable
reasoning: Ben Graham-Nellor discusses the real-world risks facing SMSF trustees as they age, including cognitive decline, death of a member, and the legal complexity of transferring trustee responsibilities. He notes that enduring powers of attorney do not automatically confer trustee status, and that a formal appointment process must occur. The ATO allows six months to restructure a fund following a member's death. He emphasises that binding death benefit nominations are essential because superannuation is not automatically an estate asset dealt with via a will. His key advice is to simplify the SMSF and put succession structures in place while all members still have full capacity.
quote: So there's a couple of things to think about South. All members of the supplemented super fund should know a few things about it. Now, quite often you do find that one member of the fund is, is kind of the chief financial officer of the fund, if you like, who's looking after everything to do with it. They know when the tax is due, they know when the audit's happening, they're paying the all the bills out of the fund. And then maybe one or two or three of the other members don't really take an active role. But it's very important that everybody understands a few things about their funds. First of all, who is the trustee? Do you have an individual trustee structure or corporate trustee structure? Because that makes a difference at the end of the day if you have to. If you have a member pass away or become incapable of running the fund, looking at who has power of attorney over the members of the fund as well. And, and remembering that holding an enduring power between it doesn't automatically make somebody else the trustee if they take over from you. But then we need to have that process in place. It's important for everyone to know who's getting the benefit, the binding death dominations, how that all works when someone was to pass away and what's going to happen to the assets within the fund.
episode_title: The SMSF risks trustees need to plan for | the advisory

When earnings are predictable and trending upward, sentiment volatility becomes an opportunity rather than a threat. So as a value investor, you can never predict the likely optimism or pessimism... But what you can do is get better and better at predicting the earnings. And in the long run, given that that sentiment will move, we talk about as a sine curve. It goes up and down, optimism to pessimism and then back. headline: Key valuation risk in loan portfolios is credit default, not mark-to-market yield movements; principal impairment drives losses, not interest rate fluctuations
reasoning: The speaker explains that while all-in yield (driven by credit quality and loan tenor) determines the theoretical market price of a loan, the real valuation risk is credit default risk rather than mark-to-market yield changes. A loan should remain worth par as long as the borrower repays in full; the danger arises when a borrower can only repay a portion of principal, resulting in a specific provision and a writedown of the asset. This distinction is important for investors evaluating private credit as a fixed income alternative.
quote: The real driver of valuation risk in a loan portfolio isn't actually the mark-to-market all-in yield, it's the risk around credit default. So if you have a position where I've lent you $100 in over the next 3 years, you're going to pay me the interest and the fees, and then in the end of 3 years, you're going to pay me back my $100. The the the loan should be worth the all-in yield as a mark-to-market price, but I should be able to be confident that I'm going to get my $100 back. If, however, you decided to not repay me my $100 or you had a had an event with that meant you couldn't repay me, and all of a sudden you could only pay me back $80, that would mean that we would effectively be potentially sustaining a loss of $20. headline: Loan valuation in private credit funds hinges on provisioning discipline and appropriate income recognition — losses crystallise when recovery falls short of par and revenue accrual must reflect expected receipts
reasoning: The speaker explains that in a credit fund, loans are marked at par as long as the borrower is expected to repay in full, but if a credit event occurs and recovery is only, say, 80 cents in the dollar, a specific provision of 20 cents must be raised and the asset carried at that impaired value. Equally important is income recognition: if a loss is anticipated, continuing to accrue the full interest and fee income would overstate fund performance and inflate the NAV or unit price. Both provisioning and revenue recognition therefore directly affect the returns investors receive and the integrity of the fund's unit price.
quote: If, however, you decided to not repay me my $100 or you had a had an event with that meant you couldn't repay me, and all of a sudden you could only pay me back $80, that would mean that we would effectively be potentially sustaining a loss of $20. The other thing that's really important in terms of valuation of loans is the recognition of revenue. And so, if you've got a In your case, you owe us $100, it would be inappropriate for me to then continue to reflect in the performance of our fund the interest and fees that you are owe me on that $100 if I think I'm going to lose less. So, again, you have to appropriately reflect the income that you're going to receive because obviously that impacts the returns an investor would receive, but also the the underlying value could impact the NAV of the fund or the unit price.

headline: Rising bond yields driven by real rates are not inherently bad for equities; it is rapid moves and inflation-driven yield rises that hurt risk markets

If yields rise because productive government spending is boosting real economic activity and productivity, equities can still perform well. She notes that the current rise is predominantly driven by real rates, which is consistent with higher equity prices, and points to the year-to-date example: US 10-year yields up ~60 basis points, S&P 500 up over 12%.
quote: It really matters why bond yields are rising when we think about the impact on risk markets. If bond yields are rising because everyone's spending loads of money, but the expectation is that that money is going to find its way into real economic activity — so the spending projects are good projects, they're going to deliver higher productivity — then bond yields can rise and not trouble the stock market. If, however, all of that spending is expected to be wasteful or find its way ultimately just into inflation rather than real activity, then that's when equity markets should be worrying.

And what we're seeing is really inflation moving through supply chains at different stages. So very basic commodities get interrupted first fuel and fertilizer and those sorts of things. And then we move through to more complex goods. So petrochemicals, plastics, PVC pipes, all those sorts of things all the way up to to much more complex, transformed, finished goods that takes longer for the inflation to show up in those items. headline: Global crude flow reshuffle underway as Venezuela barrels shift from China to US Gulf Coast and India, creating a quality-of-crude mismatch
reasoning: Sahdev explains that Venezuelan heavy crude historically required light naphtha inputs from Russia, China, and Iran, with output flowing to China. Now the US has cut that arrangement, supplying its own naphtha to Venezuela and directing output toward the US Gulf Coast. However, US Gulf refineries have a limit on heavy barrel intake, so India — with complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil capable of processing heavy, sour Venezuelan crude — becomes a beneficiary. China has effectively lost Venezuelan, Iranian, and some Russian barrels simultaneously, creating a multilayered reshuffle of crude, naphtha, and fuel oil flows he calls 'chem politics.'
quote: India in that case is a bit of a lucky advantage because India has very complex refineries like Reliance and Indian Oil, which can process the dirty, heavy, sort of toxic, I would say Venezuelan kind of crudes at an advantage price. So there is a lot of reshuffle, not just of the crude but naphtha, but fuel oil. It's, I would say not just geopolitics, I would call it. It is chem politics at play.
episode_title: Why oil’s headline rally may have more bark than bite

headline: Headline geopolitical risk overstated; dark trade, storage, and Venezuela supply check prices with $95 as likely top-end
reasoning: Sahdev argues that while oil prices are rising on headlines around US strikes on Iran and Strait of Hormuz tensions, the underlying fundamentals are less bullish than the market reaction implies. A large volume of crude is moving via 'dark trade' — with transponders turned off — meaning supply leakages are not captured in tracking data, and this hidden supply is keeping actual delivered volumes higher than official numbers suggest. US peak summer demand is over, Venezuela has ramped production toward 1.2 million barrels per day (once near 3.5 mbpd), and some Russian diesel and Caspian flows continue. He also notes voyage time uncertainty (not a supply shortage) is what keeps prices elevated, and pegs $95/bbl as roughly the top end of the range.
quote: I believe Venezuela is a noose around there. Dark trade is the news that's keeping the oil price is probably. And my guess is 95 is probably the top end... I think the attacks that were happening on Kazakhstan and some of the Caspian barrels, uh, were also have some of somehow slowed down. So, yes, I would say dark trades, uh, to some extent. Also the US, uh, summer season is over. The peak summer season is likely over now, and that probably keeps a check on the oil price.

headline: Premiums and discounts to NTA in LICs are driven by supply/demand dynamics, not just portfolio performance — dividends, shareholder communication, and buyback efficacy all play key roles
reasoning: Jesse Hamilton explains that LIC premiums and discounts are fundamentally a supply-and-demand phenomenon. Strong performance alone does not guarantee a premium, and poor performance does not guarantee a discount — shareholder communication and understanding of the investment strategy matter equally. Above-market fully franked dividend yields can attract demand and push a stock to a premium, while insufficient yield can cause persistent discounts. On-market buybacks are mathematically accretive to remaining shareholders' NTA per share but in practice do not durably close discounts because they absorb supply temporarily without creating new demand; once stopped, the supply returns. A company conducting a buyback also signals to Hamilton that management sees no better use of capital than buying back shares rather than investing in the market.
quote: People would think that they are, but in practice for listed investment companies, they don't have much of an impact. And it sounds a little bit counterintuitive. Mathematically buybacks work. You're buying back shares in the company at less than what they're worth. So the arithmetic stacks up where it actually increases the value of the NTA per share for the remaining shareholders. And I can understand why companies do it. But when you get back to why companies trade at a premium or discount, a buyback doesn't change the supply and demand dynamic. It soaks up supply, but it doesn't stop it and it doesn't create new demand. So what you tend to find is when companies might be conducting an onmarket buyback, it works for a short period of time and the minute you stop that buyback, the supply is still there and there's no new demand. So whilst buybacks sort of work in theory from a mathematics standpoint, in practice they don't work. And when I look at a company doing a buyback, the first thing that signals to me is there's no better use for the capital.
episode_title: Understanding Premiums and Discounts in Listed Investment Companies

headline: Flags that a divided government post-midterms raises debt ceiling and government shutdown risks, with distinct market implications for each
reasoning: A divided government outcome from the 2026 midterms would likely increase fiscal noise around recurring deadlines including government funding and the debt ceiling. Salvatore differentiates the market impact of each: shutdowns primarily have indirect effects by degrading or delaying government economic data, hampering decision-making by investors and the Fed. By contrast, the debt ceiling has a more direct market impact, showing up in the Treasury bill market where bills maturing near a potential X-date cheapen relative to other short-term benchmarks as investors price in default risk, even when resolution remains the base case.
quote: If we get a divided government in November, that typically means more fiscal noise around the recurring deadlines, like government funding and the debt ceiling. Those two matter for markets in very different ways. A shutdown's bigger effect tends to be indirect. So think delayed or lower-quality government data, since agencies can end up working from smaller survey samples. That leaves investors and the Fed making decisions with less complete information for weeks at a stretch sometimes. The debt ceiling is more direct. That shows up most clearly in the Treasury bill market. Bills maturing around a potential deadline tend to cheapen relative to other short-term benchmarks, as investors have to price default risk into that narrow window. And that's the case even when a resolution is still the base case.
episode_title: The Politics Behind the Rising U.S. Debt

reasoning: Stevenson draws a key distinction between demand-driven inflation and supply-shock inflation. He notes the current inflation is supply-driven (rising oil prices from the Gulf conflict) and argues it need not feed through to wage inflation as it did post-Ukraine in 2022. Labour market conditions are weaker this time — vacancies are falling, private-sector wage growth is only around 2.8%, and workers lack bargaining power. Furthermore, higher energy costs act as a deflationary force longer-term by squeezing consumer spending and reducing corporate pricing power, which could mean fewer rate rises than markets currently price in.
quote: I think that the jobs market is weaker than it was then. I think that the number of vacancies is falling. The wage inflation figures within the overall inflation figures are actually easing quite a lot at the moment. And the other argument that you can make about this external shock, this oil price shock, oil prices going up, fuel prices going up, electricity heating costs going up, in the short term that might push the inflation rate higher. But longer term, that might actually be a deflationary impulse, because people have got less money to spend. Their spending less means companies have less pricing power, they're less profitable, they're probably hiring fewer people. So I think you can make quite a strong case the opposite way, that actually inflation is less of a problem.

headline: Fidelity's Tom Stevenson explains why tracker mortgages are cheaper than fixed rates, signalling market expectations of UK rate rises
reasoning: Tom Stevenson explains that when variable/tracker mortgage rates are lower than fixed rates, it reflects the market pricing in future rate increases. Lenders offer cheaper variable rates because the interest-rate risk is borne by the borrower; for fixed rates, the lender prices in expected average rates over the fix period to protect against adverse moves. The current spread — with fixed rates spiking above 5% in 2026 while trackers remain around 4% — reflects market expectations that the Bank of England base rate will rise from 3.75% toward 4.5% over the next year or so, driven mainly by oil-price-related inflation following conflict in Iran.
quote: So if variable rates are lower than fixed rates at the moment, which is the situation you've described, that is because the market expects interest rates to rise. And so therefore the fixed rate is covering the bank against that possibility.

headline: Avoids the property development sector as too hard for compounding investors
reasoning: Property development by its nature requires constant recycling of capital: operators take risk to improve assets, then must sell or monetise and start again rather than compounding returns. This means investors face an ever-compounding element of risk rather than reward. The bigger the company gets the larger the bets required and the higher execution risk becomes. Stockland's 10-year results demonstrate this with every good year followed by excess risk in the next. Coleman also notes most Australians already have heavy property exposure through their own homes and investment properties, making additional listed property exposure redundant.
quote: the challenge in property development and property ownership from a compounding point of view if you want to think of investing as the goal of compounding growth year after year until hopefully an infinite time horizon though none of us will ever live that long is that in the property development game what they call a pipeline we as an investor have to call starting over because the nature of the business is to take something unloved put risk and capital into it to make it better and then having completed that exercise rather than sitting back and enjoying the fruits of your labor you have to either sell it or monetize it and then go again and so as an investor you are going to experience in the property sector in general in Stockland is no no unique beast in that a constantly compounding element of risk rather than reward because the bigger they get the bigger the gambles they have to take the higher the execution risk comes the more likelihood that you can't get one part of that pipeline right.
episode_title: the call: Friday 28 August

headline: Andrew Coleman avoids Zip and the buy now pay later sector as structurally dangerous lending to those banks won't touch
reasoning: Buy now pay later, private credit, subprime and B-grade lending all share the same fundamental flaw: they lend to people or companies that banks will not lend to, at rates those borrowers would never pay at a bank. As long as the economy is strong repayments continue, but at the first sign of weakness the customers in that socioeconomic band default disproportionately. External investors cannot properly evaluate the loan book quality and therefore face catastrophic information asymmetry: making one to two percent on each loan when it goes well and losing 100% when it goes badly.
quote: the challenge with any business model whether it's a buy now pay later whether it's a B grade lender whether it's private credit that involves you taking risk by giving people money who can't get that money from other easier avenues is that as long as the economy continues strongly you're probably okay that money will be repaid people don't tend to take on debts they have no intention of ever repaying the challenge is that as soon as there's any weakness in the economy the customers who repay the least the quickest are those of course who are in that socio-economic band if it's individuals or companies in that lower level of earnings band who couldn't borrow money from banks... by now pay later private credit B grade finance subprime lending whatever you want to call it it changes its name every few years is all about lending to people the banks won't lend to at rates that they would never have to pay at the bank and that means it's always a house of cards because the more you grow the more risk you take on that somewhere in your lending book is a big cohort of customers that if something goes wrong they won't be repaying.

headline: Adam Stokes says the US Clarity Act is a structural positive for crypto, unlocking bank participation, institutional confidence, and consumer protection.

Without clear rules, businesses have been leaving the US, creating a capital and brain drain in digital assets. With the Clarity Act, banks gain confidence to buy Bitcoin and offer ETFs, institutional investors gain greater certainty, and consumers receive stronger protection including anti-money laundering requirements. Stokes frames this as America's strategic decision to lead the next generation of financial technology rather than cede ground to Singapore, Dubai, Europe, or China.
quote: The biggest thing the Clarity Act provides, all of us is exactly what the name suggests clarity. For years, crypto companies have spent so much time and money asking what is the security and what is a commodity? And the answer was essentially through being sued by the SEC... What the Clarity Act attempts to do is create clear rules of the road forward. And this gives businesses confidence to invest, which trickles throughout the global economy. It also gives banks the big one confidence to participate. And we're seeing that with banks now buying Bitcoin and offering ETFs themselves to their customers, and it gives institutional investors greater confidence.

headline: Seven regulatory changes incoming for Australian SMSFs targeting fraud prevention, trustee accountability and fee transparency
reasoning: The Australian government is introducing seven changes to tighten the SMSF space. These include a requirement for a unique bank account per SMSF, a new trustee knowledge test administered by the ATO, an increased supervisory levy of $295 per year charged from inception, mandatory disclosure of the advisor who set up the fund, a separate line in tax returns for advice fees, a contribution to the compensation scheme of last resort (expected ~$20 per fund across 600,000+ funds), and a ban on cold calling by unregistered advisors including through social media platforms. Shorte views most of these positively, particularly the cold calling ban and the education/knowledge test, though notes the difficulty of policing overseas call centres. He also cautions that the supervisory levy is likely to rise over time once introduced.
quote: The ministers come out. They're trying to tighten up on the SMSF space and make sure, you know, trying to prevent some fraud and ensure people are going into them for the right reason. Um, seven really changes that will affect none of them. Absolutely major. But, um, some basic stuff like your SMS has to have a unique bank account... the supervisory levy used to be charged at the end of the first year... they're putting that up in price to $295 a year and doing it from inception... the advice fees now will have its own line in the tax returns... the Smurfs will also now have to contribute towards this compensation scheme of last resort... and then one I really appreciate is that they're going to ban cold calling by none registered advisors.

headline: Perpetual's Amy Xie Patrick not alarmed by tight credit spreads, viewing spread tightness as normal cycle behaviour rather than a sell signal
reasoning: Amy Xie Patrick argues that credit spreads historically spend most of the cycle near their tights rather than their wides, making tightness in itself a poor timing signal. She notes that Australian major bank senior five-year paper is yielding around 60–70 basis points over the swap curve, which is modest but is simply the return on offer for that risk. Unlike equities, credit does not have open-ended upside, but the seniority and structural position of credit investors also limits downside. She says the more important signal is underlying corporate and macroeconomic fundamentals rather than spread levels per se.
quote: Credit spreads behave very differently to equities, even though they're positively correlated. The major difference is that credit spreads aren't really supposed to go very far in either direction, especially in investment grade. You know, today for major bank senior paper in Australia at, say, the five-year point, you're probably getting paid something like 60 to 70 basis points over what a swap curve would give you. And that's not very much... the behavior of credit markets is that for a lot of the cycle, they stick closer to the tights than to the wides of that cycle... credit spreads being tight in and of itself, I wouldn't use that as a signal for timing or for how much you should allocate at any one point in time.

About $3 million annualised in investment is now in the rearview mirror and the company will begin shipping the new encoders in H1 FY27. Legacy human-in-the-loop services were deliberately shut down in December, ending revenue decline from that segment. Lexi Text SaaS revenue grew 42% year-on-year to $34.1 million and total revenue is expected to grow. The hardware decline of $6.4 million is attributed to customers waiting for the new encoder rather than demand erosion.
quote: I think the highlight of the full year results was really the second half, because in the first half we deliberately invested in getting all of our products up to the AI native environment, and principally that was with our core fleet of captioning encoders. And these encoders sit at the point of broadcast. And this was the first upgrade that we had done in ten years. So we resolved 37 fundamental security flaws across that architecture. And so we've got brand new AI. Native encoder platform. We will begin shipping those this half. Um, but all of the investment in getting that done, about 3 million annualized, uh, is in the rearview mirror now, which is good.
episode_title: The Lexi lift: AI-Media’s shift to AI-native growth

headline: Ai-Media's Lexi Direct software platform embeds captioning natively inside third-party broadcast ecosystems, broadening distribution beyond proprietary hardware
reasoning: Abrahams describes Lexi Direct as a software encoding platform that turns third-party hardware into an encoder, allowing Lexi to operate inside another vendor's broadcast walled garden. As an example, Ai-Media is now natively embedded within Grass Valley's AMP playout system, enabling Grass Valley customers to purchase Lexi services via Grass Valley tokens. This move is designed to take Lexi beyond hardware-only broadcast delivery into software, education, and government markets, significantly expanding the total addressable market.
quote: The other thing that we've built, which is even more fundamental, is a software encoding platform called Lexi Direct, which effectively turns somebody else's hardware into an encoder and allows Lexi to sit inside somebody else's broadcast walled garden. So, for example, Grass Valley have an AMP playout system. We are now natively embedded within Grass Valley, so if someone is a customer of Grass Valley, they can then select to pay for Lexi via their Grass Valley tokens. So it's about really getting, um, Lexi out of just a hardware delivered broadcast infrastructure, um, into hardware and software and then taking it outside of broadcast, putting it into education and putting it into government markets.
episode_title: The Lexi lift: AI-Media’s shift to AI-native growth

headline: Primary Wave CEO argues music royalties are superior to traditional credit due to inflation-positive cash flows, long duration, and uncorrelated returns
reasoning: Larry Mustal contends that music royalties outperform standard credit on multiple dimensions. The asset class is inflation-positive because royalty income rises when streaming platforms like Spotify or Apple raise subscription rates. Duration is exceptional — copyright protection extends 70 years past the death of the last writer, generating 35-40 years of visible cash flows. Returns are uncorrelated to markets because music consumption actually increases during periods of global strife. Alpha can be created through active brand management, marketing, and content creation, something most passive royalty collectors do not pursue.
quote: Music royalties are better than credit. They're better than standard credit because the reality is that these assets talking about inflation, they're inflation positive because every time Apple or Spotify or a DSP raises their rates, we're the beneficiary of them raising rates because we get a piece of that. If you look at the characteristics of the asset class, you can't match the duration of music royalties in terms of comparing it to credit because in many cases, songs don't go into public domain for 70 years after the death of the last writer on a song. This is 35, 40 years of ongoing cash flow stories. And also, where do you find credit that's uncorrelated to the market? So our best times are when there's strife in the world and people come to music for comfort, so it's uncorrelated to the markets.

headline: Andrew Coleman outlines a value-investing framework for identifying when market sentiment has overshot or undershot fundamentals using historical P/E ranges.
reasoning: Coleman explains that a reliable indicator of sentiment-driven mispricing is comparing a stock's current P/E ratio to its long-run historical range. If a stock that has historically traded at 15–20x earnings is suddenly at 50–100x, sentiment has clearly outrun fundamentals; conversely, if it has fallen to 5–10x, fear has done the same in the other direction. He argues that each dollar of earnings should theoretically command the same multiple regardless of its source, so applying a higher or lower multiple is itself a signal of emotional rather than fundamental pricing. The value investor's edge is the ability to simply wait for fundamentals and price to re-converge rather than constantly chasing narratives.
quote: If a company has traded historically on a p e ratio of between 15 and 20, you know, pretty much in law in line with the long term market average. And suddenly it's trading on 50 or 60 or 100 times earnings. You've got a pretty good factual basis to assume. Sentiment has outstripped fundamentals and vice versa. If it was trading at 15 to 20 and it's now trading at 5 to 10 in an extreme case, well then fear has clearly outstripped fundamentals because theoretically, from a value investor's point of view, each dollar should be worth the same to you as an investor, no matter where you got it from. So the second you find yourself doing that, applying a higher multiple to one thing and a lower multiple to another, it's an indicator that you at least if not the market as a whole, has got caught up in the sentiment, positive or negative rather than the fact.

headline: Lifetime income streams offer significant age pension assets and income test advantages, making early investment more beneficial
reasoning: Justine Marquet explains that lifetime income streams are assessed at only 60% of the original purchase amount under the assets test, compared to full value for account-based pensions, term deposits, shares, and managed funds — a 40% reduction. Critically, this assessed amount is based on the original purchase price and does not grow with actual investment earnings over time, meaning earlier investment locks in a more favourable base. On the income test side, only 60% of income received from lifetime income streams is assessed, providing a 40% discount, and these income streams are excluded from deeming altogether.
quote: What happens is only 60% of the purchase amount is is tested for the assets test, rather than the whole amount of the investment, which would occur with other types of financial investments, like most other assets in your account based pension or term deposits or shares or managed fund values. So that's a 40% reduction in the assets test, and that is based off the original purchase amount. And that's deemed over time. But it doesn't grow over time with the actual earnings of the investment. So you can you can get a distinct advantage by investing earlier. And then on the income side, income from lifetime income streams, uh, only only 60% of the income is assessed. So you're getting a 40% discount on the assessment under the income test. Um, that's of the actual income received. Uh, not of any deemed amount. So they're excluded from deeming altogether.
episode_title: Why a bigger pension may not mean more income | the advisory

headline: Allianz Retire+ highlights structural benefits of lifetime income streams in reducing means-tested asset and income assessments
reasoning: Lifetime income streams are not assessed as standard financial investments under Centrelink means testing; they attract a discounted assets and income test, which can meaningfully improve a retiree's age pension entitlements. The benefit is amplified the earlier a retiree invests in such products — investing pre-retirement can generate enhanced outcomes by the time retirement commences. Two retirees with identical asset levels can achieve very different retirement income outcomes purely based on how their assets are structured. This creates a significant advisory opportunity for retirees near means-test thresholds.
quote: By including a lifetime income stream as part of your retirement portfolio, uh, it can have really different outcomes because it's just not deemed as a financial investment. It has a different assets in factored. A discounted assets and income test will apply to to money that you're receiving and assets that you have in lifetime income streams that you have invested in them and and the value of those and the impact that it has on, say, age, pension and your overall retirement income can be magnified the earlier that you decide to invest in these kinds of, of products and structures. So by investing pre-retirement, you get enhanced outcomes by the time you get to retirement just because of the way the rules work.

quote: So I think the outlook for FY 27 is very strong, because some of the pricing and other initiatives we put through are really going to take effect and have a noticeable impact next year. But those are going to continue through FY 27 at the current rate. And that by itself gives us a tremendous tailwind. We also were best known for our sophistication around credit risk management. It progressively dawned on Australians that the combination of high imported share of the LNG capex and high foreign ownership meant that looking at the traditional gross domestic product (GDP) growth measure is misleading for what this meant for >99% of Australians who had nothing to do with the LNG sector. RNNDI accounts for the impact of profits accruing to offshore owners of the assets and the depreciation of those assets.

headline: Yarra's Tim Toohey argues Australia's data centre boom is vastly overstated as an economic growth driver due to the high imported content of capex.
reasoning: Toohey contends that over 80% of data centre capex is imported — primarily servers and GPUs which alone represent ~70% of total cost — meaning the domestic economic multiplier is far smaller than headline investment figures suggest. He argues bank and broker research has conflated total data centre spend announcements with construction-only cost breakdowns (e.g. Cushman & Wakefield reports), which exclude GPUs and servers entirely. On CEFC forecasts of $85–135bn in investment over the decade, he says domestic GDP impact needs to be discounted by ~80% once imports are subtracted. He further notes that economic growth is a rate-of-change concept, so ever-larger announcements are needed to sustain contributions, and there are rising concerns hyperscalers have overstepped capital market capacity. Community and regulatory pushback in developed nations is also an underappreciated risk.
quote: The likelihood that the current data centre build out will result in a material uplift in near term Australian economic growth is negligible in our view. The most obvious reason is the misconception that data centres are 'homemade'. They are not. It is reasonable to look at a large refrigerated shed and think that a lot of local economic value-add was required to build it. However, even if we assume that all the steel, roofing, site works, land acquisition, grid connection and most of the engineering design and specialist labour is domestic in nature (which frankly is a stretch), then we are still left with well over 80% of the cost of each data centre as being imported. The cost of data centre building – the thing we see with our own eyes – averages out to just 2.5% of the total capex. The cost of adding the servers and GPUs is closer to 70% of the total capex bill.
episode_title: Tim Toohey: Australia’s Data Centre Boom (a Counterview)

headline: Toohey uses Australia's LNG boom as a cautionary tale — PRRT revenue collapsed from 12% of exports in 2011 to just 2% in 2025 despite a 5x rise in LNG export value
reasoning: Toohey highlights that despite LNG export revenues increasing more than 5x since 2011, the quantum of Petroleum Rent Resource Tax (PRRT) paid has remained largely flat at around $1.5bn per annum. As a share of LNG exports, the PRRT shrank from 12% in 2011 to just 2% in 2025. Treasury forecast in 2011 that the LNG sector would generate an $11bn increase in PRRT over four years; actual receipts were less than half that figure and continued to shrink. Today the PRRT represents just 0.17% of Australian taxation revenue. Toohey uses this outcome to warn that data centre revenue projections — which lack even an equivalent royalty or rent tax — are likely to follow a similar trajectory of disappointment for Australian households and taxpayers.
quote: Despite LNG export revenues having increased by more than 5x since 2011, the quantum of PRRT paid has remained largely unchanged at around $1.5bn p.a. As a share of LNG exports, the PRRT has shrunk from 12% of exports in 2011 to just 2% in 2025. Compared to Treasury forecasts in 2011 that the LNG sector would generate an $11bn increase in the Petroleum Rent Resource Tax (PRRT) over the next four years, the tax office received less than half of that forecast revenue. The tax take continued to shrink in subsequent years. Today the PRRT represents just 0.17% of Australia's taxation revenue.

headline: Toohey warns Australia's data centre boom will deliver far less economic benefit than advertised, drawing direct parallels to the LNG investment boom
reasoning: Toohey argues that because foreign-owned hyperscalers dominate data centre ownership in Australia, the bulk of economic rent — including cloud services, AI model revenue and high-margin IP — will be booked and taxed offshore in low-tax jurisdictions, not Australia. Australian subsidiaries will likely be treated as cost centres charged back to parents at thin cost-plus margins, meaning minimal taxable profit onshore. Rapid depreciation schedules on data centre capex will further erode any pre-tax Australian profit. He draws an explicit parallel to the LNG boom, where Treasury expected an $11bn PRRT windfall but received less than half, and today the PRRT represents just 0.17% of Australian tax revenue. Without mechanisms such as Pigouvian taxes or profit-shifting safeguards, governments' projected revenue windfalls will prove illusory, and Australia will bear all the negative externalities — excess electricity and water consumption, labour market displacement — while foreign owners capture most of the upside. He characterises this as a potential 'fool me twice' moment for Australian policymakers and politicians.
quote: It should be little wonder why Australia is seen as such an attractive destination for the Hyperscaler's data centre ambitions: the LNG industry provided the blue-print. Predictably, Australian politicians have fallen over themselves welcoming the data centre boom. The LNG investment boom may well have been a case of 'fool me once'; the data centre boom is lining up as a strong case of 'fool me twice' and shame should sit with any politician who fails to recognise that the economic impacts are going to be a lot smaller than those cited by the data centre proponents. Hopes of a revenue windfall for governments will largely prove illusionary unless mechanisms are put in place to safeguard against profit shifting and potential labour market displacement.
episode_title: Tim Toohey: Australia’s Data Centre Boom (a Counterview)

headline: Toohey questions the economic rent distribution from Australia's data centre boom, highlighting that hyperscalers and foreign operators capture most value while Australia bears externalities
reasoning: Toohey notes that data centre ownership in Australia is split between foreign hyperscalers, operators who build and lease capacity (such as Equinix, Digital Realty, NextDC and AirTrunk), and a complex financing layer involving special-purpose vehicles, private credit funds and pension funds (including Blue Owl, PIMCO, Apollo and Blackstone). Statistical GDP measures capture the physical economic activity in Australia but obscure how much of the economic rent flows offshore. The higher-margin value — cloud services, AI models and software IP — sits in parent companies or low-tax jurisdictions, not Australian subsidiaries. Australia gets construction jobs, electricity revenue and minimal operational employment, but also takes on all negative externalities including grid stress, water consumption and potential labour displacement. He argues there is no data centre equivalent of even the inadequate PRRT on LNG, leaving Australia with no mechanism to share in the excess returns.
quote: Rather than focusing on how many construction workers will be required to build the data centre sheds, the real question is what proportion of the data centres are owned by foreign owned hyperscalers, what percentage is owned by operators who build and then lease capacity to the hyperscalers and enterprises (e.g. Equinix, Digital Realty, NextDC, AirTrunk etc.) and what share of the returns are diverted to an increasingly complex financing layer of special-purpose vehicles, joint ventures and private credit funds (e.g. Blue Owl, PIMCO, Apollo, Blackstone, and increasingly pension and superannuation funds). Typically, the higher-margin economic value — the cloud services, AI models, and software running on the hardware — is in the intellectual property held in the parent company or in a low-tax jurisdiction. It is highly likely the Australian data centre subsidiary will be treated as a cost centre charged back to the parent at a thin cost-plus margin. The practical result is that the host country gets some construction jobs, electricity revenue, some very small operational employment but they also take on all the negative externalities.
episode_title: Tim Toohey: Australia’s Data Centre Boom (a Counterview)

headline: Barry flags rising risk that Treasury cuts long-end auction sizes as a next step, with historical evidence suggesting strong announcement-day impact but poor durability

headline: Barry warns Treasury buyback expansion is too small to materially move rate levels and risks undermining the Treasury's credibility as a regular and predictable issuer without accompanying fiscal consolidation
reasoning: The annualized additional buyback volume of ~$64bn is modest relative to ~$5 trillion in gross coupon issuance annually and a $31 trillion market. Without fiscal consolidation, markets are likely to view the action as lacking credibility, and the move away from 'regular and predictable' debt management could increase the Treasury's long-run cost of funding.
quote: So I think it's aimed at that. And the sizing is such where it's not big enough to materially impact rate levels. Because if we look at it again, in aggregate sizing at the long end of the curve, or in aggregate, in the scope of a Treasury department that on a growth space, which is close to 5 trillion in securities per year in the coupon space, and a $31 trillion market is rather limited... With what happened yesterday, I think you can argue that this is a little bit of a move away from regular and predictable in that fashion. And the reason that matters to me is if there's no corresponding fiscal action taken, markets could view this to be lacking credibility.

headline: Barry identifies a powerful potential coordination between the Fed and Treasury via rolling Fed's maturing Treasury portfolio into the short end rather than pro-rata, avoiding rate impact while addressing debt composition
reasoning: The Fed's Treasury portfolio has an average maturity more than 2.5 years longer than the Treasury market itself, a reversal of the pre-GFC norm. Close to $2 trillion in Fed holdings will mature in coming years; currently these are rolled over pro-rata across the curve. Barry argues the Fed could instead roll maturities into short-end securities, rebalancing its portfolio to pre-crisis norms and giving the Treasury more short-end issuance without increasing supply to the public in a way that moves rates. He frames this as a more powerful and technically cleaner coordination than the buyback program.
quote: The average maturity of what the Fed owns in its Treasury portfolio is more than two and a half years longer than the average maturity in the Treasury market itself. And pre-GFC, what the Fed owned was actually shorter than the Treasury market itself. So there is close to two trillion insecurities from the Fed's portfolio maturing in the next few years. Right now, it rolls them over passively at auction across the curve, pro rata to whatever the Treasury is auctioning, as a passive participant at auction. If it decides to roll them over at the short end instead, it gets the balance sheet back to what it looked like pre-crisis. It also gets the Treasury Department more short-end issuance but not to the public in a way that does not impact rate limits. So I think that's the coordination that's very, very powerful.

headline: Barry argues US fiscal consolidation is the necessary and missing ingredient for any durable reduction in long-end Treasury yields; budget deficits at 6% of GDP during an expansion remain the core constraint

He frames the six-month test for whether yesterday's announcement was a turning point as entirely dependent on whether fiscal action follows.
quote: The bigger issue here that we've been grappling with and fiscal hasn't been a part of the conversation for over a year in the U.S. because budget deficits have been stable, but stable at 6% of GDP. So if you're going to take action on this, it needs to be accompanied by some sort of fiscal consolidation. And I think investors with what they've seen here, with rates going back to where they were, are saying we don't see the fiscal consolidation... if we're sitting here six months from now, whether it's been impactful or not is whether it's followed on with any sort of fiscal consolidation to go alongside it.

High level measures of liquidity are very close to decade highs. headline: Barry warns that elevated T-bill share of outstanding US debt — at recessionary levels during an expansion — limits the Treasury's ability to lean on the bill market in the next downturn

He is concerned that the elasticity of demand and inelasticity of pricing that make T-bills attractive in recessions may not be available to the same degree if the starting share is already elevated when the next downturn arrives.

They could do this in an unlimited fashion. The theoretically that's true. But we know that the T-bill share of outstanding debt has been on the rise for the last few years. And it is at a relatively high share now, considering we're still in an economic expansion... it's just my fear here that the starting point with the T-bill share at levels that we typically don't see except in recessions, the next time you need to lean on the T-bill market for an increase in issuance the next recession, you may not have the same benefits you had in the past.

quote: So the read-through for me, this announcement yesterday, alongside the very curious change that the Treasury Department made to its guidance that the obvious refunding two weeks ago, as well as the intervention that was done in Euro-EN, all reads that they're attempting to sort of stem the tide here in long-term rates, perhaps until they see more decisive action on the monetary normalization side from the Bank of Japan. So I think it all comes down to discomfort with rate levels, knowing that the Fed is not, I wouldn't say being uncooperative, but sees no reason to cut rates. Japan is a key factor there. It's worth maybe 20 basis points though. So yes, it's worth something. But you as the debt manager of the largest government bond market in the world, like is something like 20 basis points that should be focused on when it's kind of exogenous to what's happening and probably requires more aggressive monetary action from Japan to take that on.

reasoning: The AI capex cycle has shifted from a balance sheet story to a capital markets story, with hyperscalers now issuing across currencies via project finance and data center structures. Issuance reached $180bn year-to-date in 2026 versus $93bn in 2025 and ~$20bn per year historically. For EM, the direct competitive impact on spreads is assessed as limited in the near term, as EM sovereign net issuance remains below 2020/2025 peaks and EM-dedicated investors cannot substitute hyperscaler paper for sovereign exposure. The risk is more concentrated among global asset managers/crossover investors where EM-IG sovereign exposure is typically less than 0.5% of portfolios.
quote: Both our corporate team and our sovereign team have weighed in on this in recent weeks. As we've described it, we're seeing the AI-cap-cycle shifting from something which is really a balance sheet story not to a capital market story, as hyperscalers are tapping much deeper pools of funding across currencies, increasingly via project finance and data center structures. So this is becoming a structural credit market theme in terms of scale. The issuance has really surged 180 billion year to date and counting for hyperscalers versus 93 billion in 2025 and about 20 billion per year on average in the prior years. So the key question for EM is whether this competes in any way or disrupts EM spreads. And our quick conclusion is not meaningful, not meaningfully, at least not in the near term.

headline: PIMCO argues US labor market is not generating inflationary pressure despite falling unemployment, as compositional wage shifts dominate
reasoning: Wilding and Westwood find that the headline unemployment rate of 4.1% overstates labor market tightness because it is accompanied by a falling employment-to-population ratio — a historically unprecedented combination. The compositional shift driving this is higher-wage workers exiting full-time employment (into part-time, unemployment, or out of the labor force entirely), which drags measured wage growth lower rather than supporting it. Unlike typical recessions where lower-wage workers exit and prop up average wages, the current episode sees above-median earners leaving, subtracting from wage measures. Demographics, AI-driven labor displacement, and immigration policy tightening are identified as structural drivers of these exits. Because labor costs are a large share of input costs, PIMCO expects consumer price inflation — currently elevated — to converge toward these moderating labor cost trends over time.

Given that labor costs are a large portion of the input costs for the goods and services produced across the U.S. economy, consumer price inflation, which is now elevated, should converge to labor cost trends over time.

headline: Enright uses Microsoft's 2000-2020 two-decade case study to illustrate that fundamentals always win and that being on the right or wrong side of change is the critical variable.

From 2010 to 2020 earnings tripled again but the stock rose nine times, as Microsoft remedied those deficiencies and repositioned itself on the right side of change. Over the full 20 years, earnings and stock price moved together, validating the principle that the gap between earnings and price must eventually close. Enright uses this as a framework for thinking about AI winners and losers today.
quote: During the first decade from 2000 to 2010, the earnings tripled. Earnings went up three times. The stock price was flat. It didn't move at all. During the second decade, the earnings tripled again, but the stock price went up nine times. So what's amazing is you had this total disconnect between the earnings and the stock price during the first decade. And then you had another disconnect during the second decade, but it was in the opposite direction. And then if you look at the 20 years in totality, the earnings and the stock price did the same thing... The difference between Microsoft during the first decade, when they didn't have a mobile strategy, when they didn't have an answer for internet as a service or software as a service, they were on the wrong side of change. And so people didn't really assign them a high terminal value. During the second decade, they remedied those problems and they were on the right side of change and the stock price demonstrated that.

headline: Fidelity's Slingo outlines when to preserve ISA vs pension for inheritance: depends on relative income tax bands of giver and beneficiary
reasoning: Following the April 2027 IHT changes, the decision about which account to draw down first in retirement—if the goal is to maximise inheritance—depends critically on the income tax band of the beneficiary relative to the retiree. If the beneficiary's income tax rate is lower than the retiree's, preserving the pension is still preferable. If the beneficiary pays a higher rate of income tax than the retiree, preserving the ISA is better because inherited ISAs are not subject to income tax. A higher-rate taxpayer beneficiary receiving a pension would face both 40% IHT and 40% income tax, leaving them with only £4,500 on a notional £12,500 pension pot versus £6,000 from an equivalent ISA.
quote: The general rule you have to be thinking about is, is there a difference in the tax bans between the person who is going to be passing on the money and the person who is inheriting that money? And if there is, you have to be very careful about whether you're spending your pension first or your ISA first. So it depends heavily on circumstances. But as a general rule of thumb, you can think that you want to preserve your pension if your child's income tax band is lower than your income tax band. But you will want to preserve your ISA if your child's income tax band is higher than your own income tax band.
episode_title: Pensions & IHT: where to take your retirement money from first

headline: Fidelity's Gemma Slingo warns UK pension savers to review retirement drawdown strategy ahead of April 2027 IHT changes affecting pensions
reasoning: From April next year (2027), UK pensions will become subject to inheritance tax (IHT) for the first time, fundamentally changing the equation of which retirement pot to draw from first. Previously, pensions were IHT-exempt, making them the preferred vehicle to preserve and pass on to beneficiaries. Under new rules, inherited pensions may face a double tax hit: 40% IHT followed by income tax of 20–45% depending on the beneficiary's tax band (if the deceased was over 75). Slingo notes that despite this change, pensions broadly remain the most tax-efficient savings vehicle across their full lifecycle due to contribution tax relief and the 25% tax-free lump sum. Tactical decisions about which pot to draw down should consider the relative income tax bands of both the retiree and their intended beneficiary.
quote: So if I look at what could potentially happen from April onwards, so if we think about a situation where, for example, your mum or your dad has sadly passed away and you're inheriting their pension, you could be in a situation if they've got a pretty big estate, that first you owe IHT on that pension, so that'd be 40% immediately shrinks your pot. But that's not actually the end of it, because in some scenarios, you'll then have to pay income tax on that pension. And depending on your tax ban, that could be anywhere between 20% and 45%. reasoning: Erbo explains that Ørsted's revised strategy focuses exclusively on bottom-fixed offshore wind, having exited floating wind, green fuels, and onshore Europe. He does believe floating wind will eventually be commercially viable but thinks the timeline is significantly longer than consensus expects, particularly given current affordability pressures on consumers. The LCOE of floating is materially higher than bottom-fixed, making it unattractive unless a market has no alternative. He views the company's competitive advantage as strongest in bottom-fixed, where growth is most certain.
quote: Our view is that with the points I mentioned before about it being a global supply chain, the European supply chain can deliver the build out that we see right now. Would it be possible for you as a state, partly state owned company to buy anything else than European? If you came and just say, hey, guys, we're just going to buy Chinese turbines now. Would you keep your job? Right now, when you look at the frameworks in Europe, if Chinese turbines is not part of the mix... The reason we stepped away from floating for us is not because we don't believe, I don't believe it will come. I certainly believe it will come. But I think it's going to take more time than people expect. Is there a good business case for it? There can be one day, I don't see it right now for us at least. Back to what we talked about before, it's about affordability. It's about cheap power for the consumers. And at a point in time where there is so much in focus, then the LCOE of floating is simply significantly higher than it is for bottom fixed.

He stresses that this demand growth means both solar and offshore wind are needed, as they are complementary rather than competitive — offshore wind has higher load factors, is closer to industrial load centres, and complements solar's intermittency profile. He is not concerned about falling solar prices cannibalising offshore wind's market, given the scale of demand growth.
quote: My view is that I see a very likely scenario where the demand for electricity in Europe towards 2050 will close to double relative to where it is today. So I think sort of the electrification demand for Europe is going to be massive in the decades to come... I think the premise behind that question is that there is an either or. If you agree with me that electricity demand, it doesn't even have to double. But let's just assume that it's going to go up with 1% to 2% for the next 15 years. You need it all. You need both solar and offshore wind.

reasoning: Erbo describes receiving a stop work order on 22 August 2025 on a US offshore wind project that was 80% complete, comparing it to building a bridge and being stopped 50 metres before the toll terminal. Ørsted subsequently filed a lawsuit against the US government on 4 September. He acknowledges in retrospect that Ørsted set the bar too high at its June 2023 capital markets day, was too focused on volume rather than value, and did not exit the US fast enough when warning signs emerged. The company had spent seven to nine years obtaining permits, making the write-downs particularly damaging. He now emphasises that projects must be structured so the company can afford to step back at any given time.
quote: Should you have been in this project in the first place? Of course, Nagel and I, when you look at it now, and when you look at the implications on Earth, not only that project, but also our ocean wind project that we stepped away from in the US and our sunrise project that we are constructing now. Of course, Earth would have been better off without. That's pretty obvious. If you were to be self-critical, what would you say the mistake was? I think that the way I look at it is where I think what we should have done is that we should have been able to, we should have stepped back soon. So if I look at those sort of the, we had a capital market stay in June 23 where we set the bar high. We took the right down on ocean wind in the US in the fall of that year. We set the bar too high on the capital market stay. We were too focused on volume rather than value. And then we didn't step away fast enough when we saw starting to see the writings on the role in the US.

Therefore, for me, in the first part of my career in Ustl, we talked a lot about climate change. Nothing has changed for me on climate change. It is the same. But now, it's not only about energy security, it's also about affordability. Because what has become quite evident also because of these geopolitical events is that the cheapest solution for the energy system as a whole in Europe for the decades to come is a system that is to a large extent based on renewables.

headline: Top and middle end of Australian property market falling as sentiment deteriorates and buyers trade down rather than up
reasoning: Sam Gordon explains that the top end of the market performs well only when sentiment is high and conditions are strong; when sentiment turns negative, buyers refuse to trade up and instead look to trade down. Because the top end rose so sharply in the prior cycle, its correction distorts the median and makes the overall market look worse than it is at the lower end.

He estimates the world is still short roughly 5 million barrels per day compared to pre-conflict levels — about 5% of global supply — but this is not showing up meaningfully in crude prices. Instead, refined product prices are extremely elevated: diesel, normally at a $15–20 premium over crude, is now at a $60–65 premium, reflecting reduced refining capacity and exports from the Gulf. Russell is sceptical of Trump administration claims that more oil is flowing through Hormuz than tracking services indicate, noting that such volumes would show up in Asian import data — and they haven't.
quote: The real problem is this is showing up in refined fuel prices much more than crude prices. Even under your best case scenario, the world is still short 5 million barrels a day of what it was pre conflict. And you know that's 5% of global oil supply. And that sort of has to show up sooner or later on prices. But it's not showing up so much in oil prices. Yes they are up. But as I say product prices are extremely elevated. And that's because the Gulf is also home to a lot of refining capacity, and they are not exporting nearly as much refined products as they used to. Pre conflict barrel of diesel was normally at a premium of 15 to $20 over a barrel of crude oil. Now it's a premium of $60–65 over a barrel of crude oil. So you can see where the problem lies.

Cycle has become more important, say the last five years. Where's the economic backdrop? Is every economy going through the same motions or are they starting to diverge? sector: Fixed Income ETFs vs Direct Bond Investment
headline: Direct bond investment preferred over ETFs as large ETF inflows force managers to become price takers on new issuance rather than price makers
reasoning: Hayes flags a structural risk with bond ETFs: as inflows surge, managers are compelled to deploy capital quickly into whatever bonds are available (e.g. tier 2 issuance), which can turn them into price takers rather than price makers. In contrast, a direct investment approach allows investors to be more selective and identify where value exists in the market. Direct investors can still obtain liquidity when required while having more control over entry points and pricing.
quote: I think a lot of people don't realize that they don't just need to access it via an ETF, because one of the risks of an ETF is then if they're just getting inflows and they're needing to deploy them. And if you think about bonds, they might be needing to deploy them into the same tier two bonds that are coming out. And it will get to a point where because they just need to get set, they become a price maker versus a price, sorry, they become a price taker versus a price maker. They they just need to get those funds deployed. And so I suppose that's one reason that we really like the direct investment, because you can kind of be more choosy and you can see where you see the value out there. reasoning: Thermal satellite heat map data from blast furnaces, coke ovens, and basic oxygen furnaces across Chinese steel mills shows hot metal production — a proxy for steel output — troughed on 2 July and has since been rising consistently. Mills are ramping up capacity utilisation to meet demand through the 'Golden September' and October peak construction season before year-end subsides. Weather disruptions (torrential rains in the north, heat waves in the south) had suppressed demand but are now easing. Widnell expects iron ore to gradually climb through year-end, recovering from the year's low of around $92.85 to current levels near $96.65.
quote: So what that data is currently telling us now, that sort of hot metal production, which is the proxy for steel production in China, um, actually bottomed out on the 2nd of July. And now we can see sort of quite a consistent and gradual ramp up in activity. Um, and so we're seeing those heat signatures get bigger and bigger and bigger and more, um, more high frequency as well. And so that's telling us that they're ramping up to meet that. Those last two bastions of, um, higher sort of steel demand, um, through the back end of the year, which falls, as you said, in September and October before sort of the market sort of then subsides, um, through the end of the year. And so they're obviously ramping up production now to feed that higher demand, um, as it comes back after, you know, um, torrential rains in the north and, um, excessive heat waves in the south. So I think we're also seeing that on the on the steel price as well. There's there's better demand out there. And also that's keeping iron ore also relatively well bid as well. So that's why, you know, we've recovered from I think it was one two weeks ago where we're trading at sort of the year's lows of 9285. And that's why we're sort of $4 up. So we're sort of expecting iron ore to sort of keep gradually, um, sort of climbing through the end of the year.
episode_title: China's iron ore chess move

headline: Navigate Commodities flags China's likely orchestration of Radiant World's downfall as a strategic move to consolidate iron ore trading through CMG and tighten Beijing's grip on physical supply
reasoning: Widnell highlights that Singapore-based physical iron ore trader Radiant World, which traded around 60–70 million tonnes of physical iron ore, is under intense scrutiny, with banks and commodity trading counterparties pulling financing. He notes China has been making noise about Radiant for years and finds the timing suspicious, suggesting this is not merely about accounting irregularities. His thesis is that if Radiant exits the market, China's state-controlled CMG (China Minmetals Group) would be the primary beneficiary, as miners previously selling to Radiant would be pushed to do spot tonnes directly through CMG or its domestic platform, or onto long-term contracts. This effectively concentrates physical iron ore trade in state hands and reduces secondary market liquidity, serving China's strategic interests.
quote: I think the timing aspect is quite, quite interesting. Um, obviously, if um, sadly, it looks like sort of, uh, radiant, um, is uh, is the subject of a lot of attention at the moment and now sort of banks and what other sort of commodity traders that finance them are all backing away from them? And that's that sort of paints. It's an interesting picture in itself that, you know, they might have some, um, their own liquidity problems in terms of financing sort of iron ore, uh, trade on the secondary market. Um, obviously, if that does happen, that means a player that was trading sort of 60, 70 million tonnes worth of physical iron ore, um, might eventually sort of exit the market. So again, it then sort of constricts that secondary physical trade and, and guess who the beneficiary is. Um, you know, um CMG then push the miners that were selling to radiant to do more spot tons directly through CMG Morton through their own domestic platform, more tonnes on long term um contracts.
episode_title: China's iron ore chess move

headline: Navigate Commodities bullish on iron ore, sees price climbing to $100–$105/t by year-end on hot metal production and seasonal restocking demand
reasoning: Atilla Widnell notes iron ore has recovered from year lows of $92.85 and expects a gradual climb through year-end. He points to blast furnace production ramp-ups and satellite-confirmed hot metal production increases in China as key demand drivers. Seasonally, Q4 iron ore futures almost always trade higher than Q3 because Chinese steel mills maintain elevated operating rates to restock ahead of Chinese New Year. Thermal satellite imagery corroborates this pattern, showing higher Q4 demand versus Q3. He targets $100–$105 per wet metric tonne by year-end, which he acknowledges is relatively optimistic versus most market consensus.
quote: I'm still relatively bullish, I think, like, um, we might find some resistance at 100. I still think we could do probably 100, 105 bucks by the end of the year. Um, that's quite optimistic, but, um, yeah, never say never. Hot metal production in China and therefore iron ore consumption should keep on climbing through the end of the year, because once we get through sort of gold and September and silver October, sort of hot metal production, steel production sort of plateaus a little bit, but it still remains relatively elevated because what they're doing is they keep their maintaining higher operating rates, um, to restock in December and January ahead of Chinese New Year.
episode_title: China's iron ore chess move

headline: NAB credit strategist warns AI investment cycle risks mirroring dot-com boom, with returns not yet monetised and capital flowing in on momentum
reasoning: Fullerton argues that AI investment is one of the fastest investment cycles in history, with the Magnificent Seven hyperscalers now cash-flow negative as capex exceeds operating cash generation, forcing them into debt markets. He draws direct parallels to the dot-com boom, UK railway mania, and US auto industry overinvestment, noting that in each case total investment exceeded the ultimate size of the market opportunity. He highlights that equity prices for the Mag 7 peaked around May and credit spreads on their bonds have begun widening, signalling early investor nervousness about return profiles. The core uncertainty is whether end users will be willing to pay enough for AI services to justify the extraordinary capex being deployed.
quote: If you look at the dot-com boom, there wasn't one particular event that caused that bubble to burst. It was really investors started to get more concerned that when they were putting more money in they weren't going to get the returns. Also these companies would report really strong kind of user clicks and investor interest in their products but then the market just started to shrug that off. And I think if you go back in time and look at past cycles, the dot-com boom in the 90s is particularly relevant here as parallels. You see that a lot of investment that goes early into these themes is really momentum investing. So people look at the returns that earlier investors got, they get in on the trade, they put money in, but then what happens is they don't necessarily have transparency over the earnings, the cash flows from this business. It's a momentum trade.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Talkin’ Bout A Revolution

headline: Widening credit spreads on hyperscaler bonds flagged as leading indicator of market reality-check on AI return assumptions
reasoning: Fullerton argues credit spreads on Mag 7 hyperscaler bonds are a superior real-time gauge of market risk sentiment compared to equity prices, because credit investors focus purely on cash flow adequacy and repayment rather than upside optionality. The recent spread widening on Nvidia and other hyperscaler bonds issued in mid-2025, in a broader environment of tight credit spreads, is flagged as an early warning signal. He also highlights the structural shift of hyperscalers from cash-flow-positive to cash-flow-negative as a key risk factor forcing them into bond markets.
quote: When investors look at credit spreads, I think that's a really good way to gauge risk within the market and if credit spreads are starting to widen it does show that there is a little bit of concern over the ability of these hyperscalers to monetize their investment in the massive capex that's being spent. The hyperscalers were using their cash flow and they have now gone cash free cash flow negative, which means they're spending more of their earnings on capex and they're starting to fund that from debt.
