Advertising revenue grew more than 300% with the Nativo integration scaling commercially, while international subscription revenue grew 45% with significant untapped paid penetration in markets like Brazil and Mexico. The firm substantially reduced its holding when shares traded through the $40-$50 range in late 2025 and has recently been adding again at lower prices, with current valuation of existing operations alone providing substantial support and giving little credit to new product development or the emerging advertising business.
quote: Our portfolio positioning reflects the same distinction between price and fundamentals. We substantially reduced our holding when the shares traded through the $40–$50 range in late 2025 and have recently been adding again at lower prices. At current levels, our valuation of Life360's existing operations alone provides substantial support for the share price. That valuation gives little credit to either new product development or the emerging advertising business. Both received further support from this week's operating result. The market wanted faster monthly active user growth. We saw considerably more information than that.

reasoning: Lowe argues that as the Fed goes, so go other central banks, citing the ECB's Lagarde also signalling a lean away from forward guidance. He believes the shift away from forward guidance is structurally positive because it restores flexibility to respond to incoming data, which was lost under zero-lower-bound forward guidance regimes. He expects Fed communication to shrink in volume, noting board-level Fed speak has already dropped to near zero under Warsh.
quote: As the Fed goes, so goes all the other central banks, right? There's a reason that all of these meetings happen around the same time with some of them the exact day after the FOMC. You know, that's the importance of the Fed. I think they set a standard in a lot of ways to how central banking is approached around the world, best practices. And quite frankly, I think a lot of the central bankers are happy to not be tied and asked incessantly what they're going to do next.

headline: High and growing government debt globally undermines prospects for Fed balance sheet normalisation without banking system reform
reasoning: Lowe highlights that the combination of elevated global sovereign debt levels, political incentives to maintain high spending, and a more fragmented global economy makes meaningful balance sheet reduction structurally difficult. He notes that Basel III's zero risk-weighting of central bank reserves incentivises banks to hold them, creating a chicken-and-egg problem for reserve reduction. Tokenization of money market instruments and repo is flagged as a potential partial solution, but he concludes the process will be slow.
quote: It's even harder when we talk about a world where the amount of government debt, Treasury is certainly first and foremost, but just government debt period is significantly higher than what it was before the pandemic. And unlikely to go down for a number of reasons, whether it's weaponization from a political side of things, or the fact that we've got more fractured regional economies rather than kind of globalization. All of that is no longer supportive of a more reasonable approach to the amount of debt that we have globally.

headline: Monetary policy transmission mechanism weakened as duration extension limits Fed's ability to control long-end yields
reasoning: Lowe contends that the Fed's rate-setting power is concentrated at the short end of the curve, while financial conditions are increasingly driven by long-end yields. The shift in the economy's duration profile has reduced the effectiveness of policy rate moves, contributing to inflation remaining above target for over 60 months. He argues this structural change justifies the Warsh task force review of the Fed's operating model.
quote: I think the last three to four years from aggressive rate hikes to one where we're certainly cutting rates even though we didn't see the Phillips curve in action shows that there is a lack of effectiveness when it comes to policy. And I think that that's really evolved as the duration within this economy has changed as significantly as it has. The long end is incredibly important for financial conditions. You know, the Fed clearly, from a rate-setting perspective, is most effective at the short end.

quote: Perth Brisbane and our falling Sydney and Melbourne are recording are negative growth at the moment. So most are forecasting 5 to 10% annualized from peak to trough. Ah fall in growth. But I think there's a lot of unintended consequences around it's investors are holding stock are there's not new investment stock coming. So there's a massive issue looming for renters. We're already seeing low vacancy rates. We're already seeing rents rising. Investors in the market are looking for higher yielding properties now because their strategy has changed. headline: Blackstone's BXMA argues stock-bond correlation breakdown makes hedge funds a core portfolio allocation, replacing the role bonds once played
reasoning: Since 2022, stocks and bonds have been correlated approximately 70% of the time, meaning the traditional 60-40 portfolio fails to provide diversification in the majority of environments. The QE era post-GFC made portfolio construction look easy, but since COVID, bonds have been down 80% of the time equities are down. This structural shift means institutional portfolios are actively seeking uncorrelated return streams. Blackstone's absolute return strategies have delivered consistent double-digit net returns and have beaten a 60-40 portfolio over the period. Sophisticated endowments such as Ivy League institutions already allocate approximately 20% to absolute return as a fixed income replacement.
quote: I think the first thing is if you look at the correlation between stocks and bonds over the last 50 years, they've actually been correlated about 64% of the time. And since 2022, that number has gone up into the 70s. And what does that mean? What that means is the traditional 60-40 or 70-30 portfolio is not working 64% of the time with both asset classes moving up or moving down at the same time. And so what we have found is a lot of our clients are looking for a solution for that... bonds have been down 80% of the time that equities are down. So portfolios are crying out for a solution because ultimately, if you want to compound capital over time, you have to be able to stay invested in your equity exposures. Bonds used to allow you to do that. They no longer work.

Over the prior 110 years to 2000, income represented 56% of total returns; going forward Yarra expects income to reclaim more than half of the return equation. Demographic pressures compound the shift, with retirees doubling to ~300k per year over the next decade, lifting structural demand for sustainable income streams.

The implication is straightforward: if the reward for capital-gains falls, retail investors (40% of the ASX) will place higher value on cash income. Under the old CGT 50% discount regime, income was 48% of total returns. Over the preceding 110 years to 2000, it was 56%. Moving forward, income could certainly reclaim more than half of the return equation.

reasoning: McDougall recommends investors focus on the combination of franked yield — the most tax-effective income available to Australian investors — alongside growth. He notes that changes to the imputation system make it increasingly important to understand what returns look like after tax. He highlights that superannuation is largely untouched by these changes, but outside of super, indexation carries a minimum 30% marginal income tax rate, making the composition of returns a critical consideration.
quote: So consider looking at a combination of franked yield which is the most effective tax effective income you can receive an Australian investor along with growth. If you're seeking advice on on your investments, then ask the same question of your advisor or wherever you're seeking advice from. But also start asking the question of what does my return look like after tax? Again, that's a conversation investors should really start considering, given we've seen changes to the imputation system. And then and thirdly, we'd suggest just to understand the rules. I mean really this doesn't apply to every investor. Remember superannuation is largely untouched as a result of these changes. But even outside of superannuation, depending on your circumstances, indexation does come with a minimum 30% marginal income tax rate. So really understanding the composition of returns and what that looks like from an after tax perspective, we think is really important.
episode_title: The tax trap Richard says investors need to rethink

headline: Australia's CGT indexation changes favour high-yield franked dividend strategies over pure growth portfolios, says Hamilton12
reasoning: Richard McDougall notes the incoming CGT indexation changes represent the largest wholesale changes to CGT calculation in 25 years. Under the new indexation model, capital gains below the inflation rate (approximately 3% p.a.) are effectively tax-free. Running the numbers, a high-yield strategy returning 10% pre-tax (3% growth, 7% fully franked income) requires a pure growth portfolio to deliver 13–17% pre-tax to achieve the same after-tax outcome. This makes pure growth strategies significantly harder to justify on an after-tax basis, as that level of outperformance is well above long-run ASX 200 average returns and requires taking on additional risk. McDougall recommends investors focus on diversified portfolios combining growth in line with inflation with majority returns from fully franked dividends.
quote: If you think of the indexation model what that means is any returns are underneath the inflation rate are effectively tax free. So if you look at an inflation rate of say, 3%, to keep things really simple, anything under 3% per annum is effectively going to be tax free from a capital gains perspective. Now we've run the numbers on this in terms of looking at, say, a high yield strategy relative to a growth strategy. If you keep it really simple and look at 10% as a pre-tax return. So if you look at a high yield strategy that, for example, is 10% pre-tax, 3% of that is growth. So effectively in line with inflation. And then the balance of the 7% is fully franked income. You actually need to achieve on a pure growth strategy to achieve the same after tax return. You need to be looking at anywhere from 13% pre-tax to 17% pre-tax on a pure growth strategy to receive the same after tax outcome as, say, a 3% and 7% yield.
episode_title: The tax trap Richard says investors need to rethink

headline: Franking credits remain a highly tax-effective income mechanism for Australian investors under the new CGT regime
reasoning: McDougall describes franking credits as widely misunderstood but fundamentally simple: corporate tax acts as a prepayment of personal tax. For an investor on a 47% marginal rate receiving a franked dividend, 30% of the tax has already been paid at the corporate level, leaving only a 17% top-up. For retirees on 0% tax, the full 30% is refunded as excess franking credits. For corporate investors, the franked dividend arrives with no additional tax liability. McDougall argues franking attached to ordinary ASX-listed shares is a uniquely effective mechanism to boost after-tax returns and should be prioritised in portfolio construction given the incoming CGT changes.
quote: Franklin is mostly misunderstood. It's actually really simple. If you think of corporate tax as a prepayment of personal tax. So, for example, if a company, um, declares they're going to pay out a dollar of which $0.70 would be a frank dividend to the investor. 30% of that is going to the ATO. Now, if that's by way of a franked dividend, um, if you're an investor on a 47% marginal tax rate, 30% of the tax on that income has already been paid. So you're only paying 17% tax on that $0.70. Conversely, if you're a retiree, for example, on 0% tax, you're going to get all of that tax back from the tax department by way of an excess franking credit.

headline: Hamilton12 recommends diversified high-yield portfolios combining franked income with inflation-level growth, not blind yield chasing
reasoning: McDougall cautions against blindly chasing yield, referencing Westpac's performance on the day as an example of the risks of concentration in a single sector. He recommends diversified yield across sectors, with a portfolio strategy that maintains growth roughly in line with inflation while generating the majority of total returns from fully franked dividends. This approach is positioned as superior from an after-tax perspective to a pure growth portfolio, particularly in light of the new CGT indexation rules taking effect in July of the following year. He explicitly warns against portfolios heavily weighted to growth stocks, which carry more risk and require higher pre-tax returns to match after-tax outcomes.
quote: Look, um, look, I don't just chase yield blindly. I mean, we would always suggest focus on diversified yield. Naturally. I mean, look what happened with Westpac today. If you're focusing on a portfolio of high yield companies in a certain sector, you can effectively open yourself up to specific stock or sector traps. So we would always suggest look at a diversified portfolio across sectors and certainly look for a strategy to take into account if we're looking at indexation. Look for a strategy that's still got growth, that's providing income not at the expense of growth, but look for a strategy that's got growth somewhat in line with inflation, where the majority of that total return is coming by way of franc dividends.

Regulatory pressure is also intensifying, with ASIC identifying ~A$270 million in fees charged to low-income customers by CBA and Bankwest. The firm characterises the banks as 'grossly profitable, economically deleterious and less intelligent,' signalling a bearish structural view.
